#*Crying a lot
#*Farting
#*Burping<ref>http://www.thebump.com/a/gas-pain-baby</ref>

#*Move your baby’s legs gently so you don’t hurt her.
#*Talk to your baby while you’re moving her legs. This may distract her from her pain and also comfort her.

Add food back in as you realize it doesn’t cause gas.<ref>https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/diapers-clothing/Pages/Breaking-Up-Gas.aspx</ref> For example, cut out foods most likely to cause allergies like dairy, peanuts, tree nuts, soy, wheat and fish.<ref>http://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/colic/basics/lifestyle-home-remedies/con-20019091</ref>

removed: Infant gas is caused by swallowing a lot of air, often as a result of crying a lot or from the breakdown of bacteria from the food the baby has consumed. It can be harder for baby to pass the gas but usually baby will manage it and in most cases, it's not something that upsets the baby much. For those times when you perceive that the baby might have gas and isn't effectively passing it though, you may need to intervene, to relieve the pressure that might be causing pain.
#Notice when your baby is suffering from gas. Typical symptoms include:[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 1.jpg|center]]
#*Fussing and crying more than usual
#*Belching, burping, hiccuping more than you'd usually expect
#*A lot of flatulence (farting)
#*Appearance of stomach pain or cramp; a hard and bloated belly may be present
#*Spitting or coughing up more undigested food than usual.

#Allow a few seconds to let the baby pass gas unaided by you. Passing gas is normal and not all fretting and fussing is gas-related. Moreover, most gas will pass unaided by you, and it's important to let the baby pass gas naturally as often as possible. Expect fussing for a few seconds, then a return to a happy or non-distressed baby. If distress continues, then you may need to intervene.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 2.jpg|center]]
===  Feed the baby in the right position ===

#Feed your baby before she cries. If the baby is given a long time to cry, then fed on top of a long bout of crying, it's probable that she or he will have a lot of air building up inside and this can lead to gas.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 3.jpg|center]]
#Aim to keep the baby's head higher than his or her stomach when feeding. This is the same whether you're breastfeeding or bottle feeding.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 4.jpg|center]]
#*Make adjustments with a pillow or cushion if you find holding the baby difficult. This will give you added support to keep the baby in a good feeding position.

#Feed slowly. Try not to rush feeding the baby. By feeding slowly and gently, the baby has time to digest the food without taking in gulps of air.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 5.jpg|center]]
#*Use a slow-flow nipple if bottle-feeding. This can help to reduce the intake of air that contributes to gas.
#*If breastfeeding, and you feel a sudden burst of milk, it can be useful to remove the baby briefly, then reset him or her to feed when the milk settles back to a slower flow.

#Try automatic tummy time after feeding. If you find that your baby is often gassy, try giving her or him some tummy time after each feed. This will allow the baby to apply direct pressure to the stomach and hopefully allow the gas to release.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 6.jpg|center]]
===  Burping holds ===

#Do the football/gas/colic hold.  To do this, place the baby's stomach down on your lower arm. This will not relieve the baby of gas but will make the baby feel better because your arm is pressing against her or his stomach. When the baby's arms and legs dangle, she or he is finally relaxing.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 7.jpg|center]]
#Do the over the shoulder hold.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 8.jpg|center]]
#*Hold baby by the bottom.

#*Bring the baby's body over your shoulder until his or her stomach is on your shoulder. You may think the baby is uncomfortable but the baby is fine because your shoulder provides a way to compress the stomach. Pressure on the stomach helps to move the gas upward and out.
#*Place a burp cloth on your shoulder.
#*Begin to tap baby's back gently.
#*Do this as much as you feel necessary. Baby will pass gas by burping, relieving the stomach pains.
===  Leg circles ===

#Place the baby on a soft surface. A bed or a sofa make good surfaces, just be sure that the baby won't fall off. Or, curl the baby on your stomach.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 9.jpg|center]]
#Hold his or her legs gently. Circle them around as if the baby were riding a bicycle.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 10.jpg|center]]
#Repeat this a few times. This movement can often help to relieve the gas pressure and allow it to come out.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 11.jpg|center]]
===  Massaging baby ===
#Place the baby on his or her back.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 12.jpg|center]]
#Gently massage the baby's stomach in a clockwise motion.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 13.jpg|center]]

#Wait for the gas to release. This can be a lovely bonding time, a chance for touch and for distracting the baby from any discomfort that the gas may be causing.[[Image:Help Relieve Gas in Babies Step 14.jpg|center]]
== Tips ==
* There are mixed reviews and no real scientific evidence for the benefits of such remedies as gripe water or over-the-counter solutions for gas in babies.

* Consider what food your baby is eating. Some babies cannot tolerate fruit juice or cow's milk and these can be a source of excess gas. Also, the usual gas-producing foods such as legumes, beans and cruciferous vegetables might be an issue. Any dietary changes should be discussed with your doctor first.
* Your baby may have an allergy or food sensitivity that is causing excessive gas. Ask your doctor for specific advice.
* There are different styles of baby massage; it's recommended that you borrow a book on baby massage techniques to learn in greater detail and find what suits you and your baby best.
== Warnings ==
* Realize that a baby passing gas can be more upsetting for the carer than for the baby! It can look painful or exasperating at times but it is a normal process.
* Whichever way you hold your baby, always ensure that you have a good hold and do not allow the baby's head to flop.

* Know when to see the doctor. See your doctor if any of these symptoms occur: your baby stays distressed for a long time, your baby has diarrhea or unexpected bowel movement changes, you see blood in the stools or vomit, your baby cries excessively and cannot be consoled, your baby has a fever, your baby stops eating, or for any concern you have about the situation.
* http://www.webmd.com/parenting/baby/crying-colic-9/infant-gas – research source
* http://www.parents.com/baby/care/gas/best-remedies-for-gas-reflux/ – research source

added: Infant gas is caused by swallowing a lot of air, often as a result of crying a lot or from the breakdown of bacteria from the food the baby has consumed. It can be harder for baby to pass the gas but usually baby will manage it and in most cases, it's not something that upsets the baby much. For those times when you perceive that the baby might have gas and isn't effectively passing it though, you may need to intervene, to relieve the pressure that might be causing pain.
# Notice when your baby is suffering from gas. Typical symptoms include:
#*Fussing and crying more than usual
#*Belching, burping, hiccuping more than you'd usually expect
#*A lot of flatulence (farting)
#*Appearance of stomach pain or cramp; a hard and bloated belly may be present
#*Spitting or coughing up more undigested food than usual.

# Allow a few seconds to let the baby pass gas unaided by you. Passing gas is normal and not all fretting and fussing is gas-related. Moreover, most gas will pass unaided by you, and it's important to let the baby pass gas naturally as often as possible. Expect fussing for a few seconds, then a return to a happy or non-distressed baby. If distress continues, then you may need to intervene.
=== Method 1: Feed the baby in the right position ===

# Feed your baby before she cries. If the baby is given a long time to cry, then fed on top of a long bout of crying, it's probable that she or he will have a lot of air building up inside and this can lead to gas.
# Aim to keep the baby's head higher than his or her stomach when feeding. This is the same whether you're breastfeeding or bottle feeding.
#*Make adjustments with a pillow or cushion if you find holding the baby difficult. This will give you added support to keep the baby in a good feeding position.
# Feed slowly. Try not to rush feeding the baby. By feeding slowly and gently, the baby has time to digest the food without taking in gulps of air.
#*Use a slow-flow nipple if bottle-feeding. This can help to reduce the intake of air that contributes to gas.
#*If breastfeeding, and you feel a sudden burst of milk, it can be useful to remove the baby briefly, then reset him or her to feed when the milk settles back to a slower flow.

# Try automatic tummy time after feeding. If you find that your baby is often gassy, try giving her or him some tummy time after each feed. This will allow the baby to apply direct pressure to the stomach and hopefully allow the gas to release.
=== Method 2: Burping holds ===

# Do the football/gas/colic hold.  To do this, place the baby's stomach down on your lower arm. This will not relieve the baby of gas but will make the baby feel better because your arm is pressing against her or his stomach. When the baby's arms and legs dangle, she or he is finally relaxing.
# Do the over the shoulder hold.
#*Hold baby by the bottom.

#*Bring the baby's body over your shoulder until his or her stomach is on your shoulder. You may think the baby is uncomfortable but the baby is fine because your shoulder provides a way to compress the stomach. Pressure on the stomach helps to move the gas upward and out.
#*Place a burp cloth on your shoulder.
#*Begin to tap baby's back gently.
#*Do this as much as you feel necessary. Baby will pass gas by burping, relieving the stomach pains.
=== Method 3: Leg circles ===
# Place the baby on a soft surface. A bed or a sofa make good surfaces, just be sure that the baby won't fall off. Or, curl the baby on your stomach.
# Hold his or her legs gently. Circle them around as if the baby were riding a bicycle.
# Repeat this a few times. This movement can often help to relieve the gas pressure and allow it to come out.
=== Method 4: Massaging baby ===
# Place the baby on his or her back.
# Gently massage the baby's stomach in a clockwise motion.
# Wait for the gas to release. This can be a lovely bonding time, a chance for touch and for distracting the baby from any discomfort that the gas may be causing.
== Tips ==
* There are mixed reviews and no real scientific evidence for the benefits of such remedies as gripe water or over-the-counter solutions for gas in babies.

* Consider what food your baby is eating. Some babies cannot tolerate fruit juice or cow's milk and these can be a source of excess gas. Also, the usual gas-producing foods such as legumes, beans and cruciferous vegetables might be an issue. Any dietary changes should be discussed with your doctor first.
* Your baby may have an allergy or food sensitivity that is causing excessive gas. Ask your doctor for specific advice.
* There are different styles of baby massage; it's recommended that you borrow a book on baby massage techniques to learn in greater detail and find what suits you and your baby best.
== Warnings ==

* Know when to see the doctor. See your doctor if any of these symptoms occur: your baby stays distressed for a long time, your baby has diarrhea or unexpected bowel movement changes, you see blood in the stools or vomit, your baby cries excessively and cannot be consoled, your baby has a fever, your baby stops eating, or for any concern you have about the situation.
* Whichever way you hold your baby, always ensure that you have a good hold and do not allow the baby's head to flop.
* Realize that a baby passing gas can be more upsetting for the carer than for the baby! It can look painful or exasperating at times but it is a normal process.
